title: Procrastination Tops Academic Struggles, Study Finds
paragraphs: You've got an important project due at school in two weeks' time. You tell yourself you'll start today. But instead of getting started, you find something else to do. And suddenly it's midnight, and you're tired — another day has passed, and you still haven't started.
Procrastination is something most of us experience. But a new study suggests that for university students, it can be one of the biggest obstacles to academic success.
A study led by Itamar Shatz, a researcher at the University of Cambridge, analyzed survey responses from more than 65,000 US college students.
More students named procrastination as affecting their academic performance than any other problem.
Nearly half said it harmed their ability to study or complete assignments. In fact, more students reported problems with procrastination than with anxiety, depression or financial worries.
But procrastination isn't simply about missing deadlines — it can create a vicious cycle that's difficult to escape.

A student who keeps putting off starting a challenging project may become increasingly stressed as the deadline approaches. That stress can affect their sleep, leaving them too tired to concentrate the next day.
So they put off starting the project again, and the cycle continues.
But why do people keep putting things off, even when it causes problems?
Fuschia Sirois, a professor at Durham University, told The Guardian that procrastination is often a way to avoid the uncomfortable feelings that come with doing a difficult task.
Putting off difficult work can provide temporary relief. But eventually, feelings of guilt, shame and stress return, potentially damaging a person's health and well-being.
And despite what many people believe, procrastination isn't necessarily a sign of laziness.
Shatz explained that even highly motivated people can struggle with it because of perfectionism, distractions or burnout.
He believes universities should do more than encourage students to learn better time management, and that they should offer support that addresses the reasons behind procrastination.
Fortunately, he added, research suggests that interventions designed to tackle procrastination can help.
